answers.answer:
Short answer: SCOPe puts the A-subunit bulge domain in the barrel-sandwich hybrid fold (b.84) but gives it its own superfamily rather than filing it as a family inside the Single hybrid motif (b.84.1), Rudiment single hybrid motif (b.84.2) or Duplicated hybrid motif (b.84.3) superfamilies. That placement asserts shared topology only, and explicitly declines to assert common ancestry.

What the bulge domain is. In V-type/A-type ATP synthase A subunits (e.g. Pyrococcus horikoshii A subunit, PDB 1VDZ/1VDY; Thermus thermophilus and Enterococcus hirae A3B3 structures later), the N-terminal beta-barrel (the region homologous to the F1 alpha/beta N-terminal barrel, b.49.1) carries a roughly 80-90 residue insertion, the 'non-homologous region' or bulge, that F1 beta subunits lack. The rest of the A subunit is split by SCOPe into the usual three domains: b.49.1 N-terminal barrel, c.37.1 P-loop nucleotide-binding domain (the extended AAA-ATPase family), and the a.69.1 C-terminal helical domain. The bulge is cut out as a fourth, separate domain. Structurally it is a sandwich of two half-barrel-shaped beta-sheets, which is exactly the definition of fold b.84, so at fold level it is grouped with the biotinyl/lipoyl carrier domains (b.84.1.1), biotin-carboxylase C-terminal-like domains (b.84.2) and the duplicated-motif domains such as the M23 peptidase (LytM/lysostaphin) catalytic domains (b.84.3).

Why it is a separate superfamily. SCOPe's levels encode different evolutionary strengths. Family means clear homology (significant sequence similarity, or very close structure plus function). Superfamily means probable common origin inferred from structural and functional features even without detectable sequence similarity. Fold means only that the major secondary structures have the same arrangement and topological connections; SCOP/SCOPe state that fold-level similarity can arise from physics and chemistry favouring certain packings, so it need not imply a common ancestor. For the bulge domain, the evidence that would justify a superfamily merger is absent: (1) no detectable sequence similarity to any lipoyl/biotinyl carrier domain or to the rudiment or duplicated motifs; (2) no shared functional feature, in particular none of the conserved lysine/hairpin-tip motif that defines the carrier domains, no metal-binding or catalytic site like the M23 peptidases, and no cofactor; (3) a completely different biological and genomic context, namely an insertion inside a P-loop ATPase catalytic subunit of a rotary motor, with a proposed structural role in the A/B interface and in coupling of the A3B3 ring with the central stalk; (4) different phylogenetic distribution, present only in V/A-type A subunits (archaea, eukaryotic V-ATPase, and a few bacteria), and absent from the F1 beta subunits that are otherwise its closest relatives. Because the A subunit's own homologs (F1 alpha/beta) lack the insertion, the bulge is best interpreted as a lineage-specific acquisition, and SCOPe has no basis to say which (if any) b.84 lineage it was acquired from. Hence it is kept as its own superfamily containing a single family, with the A-subunit bulge domains as the only members.

The evolutionary claim that placement makes. Placing it in b.84 at fold level says: 'this domain has the same barrel-sandwich hybrid architecture as the hybrid-motif superfamilies.' Putting it in a distinct superfamily says: 'we do not claim it is homologous to any of them.' Equivalently, the classification is agnostic between convergent evolution of the hybrid-motif topology and a divergence so ancient that no sequence or functional signal survives. It also makes the positive claim that all A-subunit bulge domains (across archaea, eukaryotic V1 A subunits, and bacterial V/A-type enzymes) are homologous to each other, which is the one family inside the superfamily.

Practical limits that follow. Function transfer across the fold is unsafe: one must not infer lipoyl/biotinyl attachment, carrier function, or peptidase activity for the bulge from its b.84 neighbours, and conversely nothing about ATPase coupling should be read into the carrier domains. Template use is limited to coarse backbone topology; sequence-based alignment or profile/HMM searches will not bridge the bulge to b.84.1/b.84.2/b.84.3, so a b.84.1 lipoyl domain is not a homology-modelling template for the bulge. Representative selection must respect the superfamily boundary: a non-redundant b.84 set at superfamily level should include a bulge-domain representative (e.g. the P. horikoshii A subunit bulge domain from 1VDZ) in addition to representatives of the three hybrid-motif superfamilies, and the fold-level grouping should not be used as a homology-level cluster. Finally, the exact numeric superfamily identifier assigned to the bulge superfamily within b.84 should be confirmed against the current SCOPe release (I recall it as the fourth b.84 superfamily, b.84.4, but am stating this from memory); the qualitative placement, separate superfamily inside fold b.84, is the point that matters.
